rules.statement: Deliver authorization responses through registered response-mode handlers resolved by name, and never hard-code a switch or a validation list over `query`, `fragment` and `form_post`.
rules.why: Response modes are an open vocabulary. A package must be able to add a mode such as `web_message` by registering a handler, without editing the library.
rules.check: Look for `switch`/`if` chains over response_mode string values, or a `response_mode` setting or validation rule that enumerates allowed modes instead of accepting any whitespace-free name.

rules.statement: Register built-in implementations of an extensible, multi-implementation service with `TryAddEnumerable`, so that packages can add their own alongside them.
rules.why: Handlers form an open set. Packages add to it by registration, and the built-ins must not block or duplicate those additions.
rules.check: Look for built-in handler or plugin registrations that use `AddSingleton`/`TryAddSingleton` for a service resolved as `IEnumerable<T>` instead of `TryAddEnumerable`.

rules.statement: When composing a registry of named handlers, validate the set as a whole once and refuse duplicate names, conflicting claims to the same role, and dangling references to names that no handler serves.
rules.why: Composing once lets the registry check the whole vocabulary up front, so a misconfiguration fails at startup and not during a request.
rules.check: Look for handler registries built from `IEnumerable<T>` with `ToDictionary` overwrites, last-wins behavior, or lazy lookups that would silently accept duplicate or dangling handler names.

rules.statement: Have a handler declare its behavioral traits as explicit properties, and never infer them from its name, such as a `.jwt` suffix check.
rules.why: Inferring traits from a name is brittle and hides the rule.
rules.check: Look for `EndsWith`/`StartsWith`/`Contains` checks on a handler or mode name that decide its behavior, such as whether it is secured or delivers in the query.

rules.statement: When no registered handler serves the requested response mode, or the tenant's `response_modes_supported` refuses it, answer `400` without redirecting. When a request object names an unserved mode, answer `invalid_request`.
rules.why: An unserved mode cannot carry even an error back to the client, so the server must not redirect.
rules.check: Look for unsupported or unserved response-mode errors that are redirected to the client, or that fall back to a default mode.

rules.statement: Apply `response_modes_supported` both to the response_mode value as written (so `jwt` must be listed to be requested) and to the resolved mode, whether explicit or default, and check it once, when the delivery is derived.
rules.why: Narrowing must cover both the shorthand and what it resolves to, or a tenant could be served a mode it did not allow.
rules.check: Look for narrowing checks that test only the raw requested value or only the resolved value, skip defaulted modes, or repeat the check in several places.

rules.statement: Never deliver a token-returning response type through a query-string response mode, including `query.jwt`, and resolve the `jwt` shorthand to `fragment.jwt` for token or ID-token response types and to `query.jwt` otherwise.
rules.why: A token never travels in a query string, even inside a JWT (JARM §2.3.4).
rules.check: Look for response-mode checks that refuse plain `query` but allow `query.jwt` for token-returning response types, or `jwt` resolution that ignores the response type.

rules.statement: Issue a JARM response JWT with `iss` set to the issuer, `aud` set to the `client_id` and `exp` counted from `iat` by a short configured lifetime. Include as claims every response parameter except the RFC 9207 `iss`, and secure error responses the same way.
rules.why: The JWT lets the client verify where the response came from and that it is intact. The RFC 9207 `iss` is the JWT's own `iss`, and errors need the same protection.
rules.check: Look for response JWTs that are missing `aud`/`exp`, that duplicate `iss` as a claim, or for error paths that bypass JWT securing in a `.jwt` mode.

rules.statement: Always sign a JARM response with the client's registered algorithm, within asymmetric-only ceilings, and encrypt it only when the client registers an encryption algorithm.
rules.why: Protection follows the client's registered metadata, as for other JWTs addressed to a client.
rules.check: Look for unsigned JARM responses, symmetric algorithms allowed in the authorization signing or encryption ceilings, or encryption applied regardless of client registration.

rules.statement: Select a response's signing and encryption credentials when the delivery is derived, before the user authenticates. Treat a credential that cannot be selected as a non-redirected `server_error` (`500`), and never fall back to weaker protection.
rules.why: Selecting credentials at write time would fail after the user authenticated and a code was issued. A response must never be sent with weaker protection than the client registered.
rules.check: Look for key or algorithm selection inside the response writer or handler, or for fallbacks that send a response unsigned, unencrypted or with a different algorithm when selection fails.
